source: Schoenfeld (1982) Expert and novice mathematical problem solving, NSF final report (ERIC ED218124)
finding: Primary source for the wild goose chase count. Twelve pretest protocols (six student pairs, two problems each) came before a month-long problem-solving course. Seven of the twelve pretests were of the Reading/Exploration type with no real planning or progress checks. Only two of the twelve posttests were of that type.
numbers: Pretest 7/12 (58%) vs posttest 2/12 (17%). This is the '60% to under 20%' figure. Unit is protocols, not students. N = 6 pairs, 12 protocols each time. No test statistic given for this count.
quote: Seven of the twelve pretest protocols were of the type (Reading/Exploration); Only two of the twelve posttest protocols were of that type.
limits: Tiny sample; pre-post with no control group for this count; coder was the author (assistants helped); counts protocols not people. Posttest managerial quality still described as quite poor. No independent replication of the count found.
agent_relevance: Closes GAP 2. The wild goose chase effect is a case-study count, not a powered experiment. Treat it as a design motivation for progress checks, not as an effect size to forecast.

source: Schoenfeld (1982) NSF final report: problem-solving course vs computer-course control
finding: A separate part of the same report compared a month-long problem-solving course with a computer-programming course (control) on a mathematics problem test.
numbers: Experimental mean 21 before, 73 after. Control mean 14 before, 24 after. Interaction F(1,17)=48.2, p<.001; term effect F(1,17)=47.5; group effect F(1,17)=130.6. Combined novice group n=19.
limits: Very small groups; same author ran course and test; test is his own; how students were assigned to course types is not clear in the text read.
agent_relevance: Shows the course effect on solving was large in a small sample, while the wild goose count (d01) is a separate descriptive number. Do not merge them.

source: Schoenfeld (1981) Episodes and executive decisions in mathematical problem solving (ERIC, same archive series)
finding: Protocol analysis of two students on the triangle-in-a-circle problem. They spent the whole 20 minutes calculating one area without ever judging whether it would help. Progress was never reassessed, so nothing could stop the chase. An expert who ran into trouble said this is too complicated, the problem should not be this hard, and changed course.
numbers: Single protocol (20 minutes); the pretest set was 12 protocols from six pairs (see d01). Expert protocol: a monitor rarely more than a minute without a control check.
quote: Progress is never monitored or (re)assessed, so that there is no reliable means of terminating wild goose chases once they have begun.
limits: Case study. The expert remark is a sign of a 'hard problems are not this hard' belief used as a stop signal, the mirror of the 5-minute belief.
agent_relevance: Names the missing control act: assess the utility of a plan before starting it, and re-assess on a clock. Maps to S6 checkpoints.

source: Lester, Garofalo & Kroll (1989) The role of metacognition in mathematical problem solving: a study of two grade seven classes (ERIC ED314255)
finding: Twelve weeks of metacognition-focused problem-solving instruction, about 3 days a week, in two grade 7 classes. A written five-problem test gained in both classes. Authors flag a ceiling effect in the advanced class and there is no control group. Belief barriers appeared in class: a group refused to try a percent problem because they said they could not do percents. Authors conclude instruction works best when prolonged and embedded in daily maths.
numbers: Regular class N=22: pretest mean 4.73, posttest 6.00 (max 10). Advanced class N=34: 6.74 to 8.38. Four advanced students scored 10 on pretest, two on posttest. The orientation category (orient, organise, execute, verify) had the most important effect.
limits: No control group; no significance test seen for the gain in the text read; ceiling effect; one teacher-investigator; belief change judged by interview, not scaled.
agent_relevance: Closes GAP 7 in part: the best-measured classroom belief work is weak evidence. Its useful rule is orientation first, and you need something to monitor. Analogue: plan and size the task before executing.

source: Dokme, Reichman & Heck (2026) TEMPER: Testing Emotional Perturbation in Quantitative Reasoning (COLM 2026)
finding: 5,400 verified emotion-neutral problem pairs from GSM8K, MultiArith and ARC-Challenge, 18 models from 1B to frontier. Emotional rewording lowers accuracy even though numbers are unchanged. Neutralising the emotional text recovers most of the loss.
numbers: Drop 2 to 10 pp. Open-source mean drop under base prompting: MultiArith 2.9, GSM8K 5.1, ARC 6.2. With zero-shot CoT GSM8K drop 4.2; few-shot CoT 4.5. Per emotion mean drop: anger 2.6, joy 1.9, sad 4.1, fear 5.2, disgust 6.4, surprise 2.4. GSM8K fear 6.1, disgust 6.1. Neutralisation recovers 70% overall (GSM8K 66%). Frontier average GSM8K base 96.5 original vs 94.2 emotional vs 95.0 neutralised; GPT-5.4 97.0 vs 95.8.
limits: Emotion is in the problem text (user side), not a pre-prompt telling the agent to feel anxious. Frontier drops are near noise (authors say GPT-5.4 approaches the noise floor). Emotional rewrites were LLM-made and 2% of neutralisations changed meaning.
agent_relevance: Closes part of GAP 5: affect in the problem statement costs 2 to 10 pp, fear and disgust most. An agent can strip emotional wording as a first step. This is about input affect, not about the agent's own anxiety.

source: Dokme et al. (2026) TEMPER controls: length-matched paraphrase, gross-neutral text, ignore-emotion system prompt
finding: Length-matched non-emotional paraphrases (900 samples, 18 models, base and CoT) caused no systematic drop, so the loss is not from longer or reworded text. A gross but neutral condition with visceral content but no emotion words cost about 3.5 points. A system prompt telling the solver to ignore emotional language was not reliable.
numbers: Paraphrase: no systematic drop. Gross neutral: about -3.5 pp. Ignore-emotion system prompt on 8 models: helped 2, neutral for 1, increased the drop for 5. Failure type attention competition: 30.0% of failures in the emotional condition vs 4.5% in originals. Emotional failures had higher classifier confidence (0.726 vs 0.691).
limits: Control is for the problem text, not for EmotionPrompt-style suffixes. Failure-pattern table uses Sonnet 4.6 plus four small models.
agent_relevance: Closes GAP 4 for the harmful direction: a length-matched neutral control exists and shows the harm is from affective content, not length. Telling an agent to ignore feelings is not a fix; rewrite the input instead.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) Do Emotions in Prompts Matter? Effects of Emotional Framing on Large Language Models
finding: First-person emotional prefixes (six emotions) before questions, tested on Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.3-70B, DeepSeek-V3.2 (GPT-OSS in the appendix) across six benchmarks including GSM8K. Static prefixes mostly change accuracy by small amounts. GSM8K and MedQA stay very close to baseline. Position of the cue matters little; paraphrasing the question hurts more.
numbers: GSM8K baselines 94.97 (DeepSeek), 94.67 (GPT-OSS), 95.00 (Llama), 93.93 (Qwen3). Prepended emotion cases stay within about -1.8 to +0.5 pp of baseline (for example GPT-OSS anger 92.87, fear 93.33; DeepSeek sad 95.42). Paraphrased variants fall to 86.66 to 93.47 (surprise lowest). Temperature 0. Adaptive selection (EmotionRL) beats fixed prompting.
limits: No length-matched neutral filler control; compared only with no prefix. Prefixes are GPT-4o-written first-person statements, not the EmotionPrompt stimuli. Single run at T=0.
agent_relevance: Closes GAP 4 on 2025-2026 models: emotional framing is a weak, mostly null lever on math. Do not put EmotionPrompt phrases in the schema as an accuracy lever.

source: Vaugrante et al. (2024) A looming replication crisis in evaluating behavior in language models? Evidence and solutions
finding: Conceptual replication of EmotionPrompt on newer models (GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Claude 3 Opus, Llama 3 8B and 70B) found no significant gain. They also argue the original 115% headline came from cherry-picking the best of 11 stimuli per task.
numbers: Overall change with EmotionPrompting +1% (chi2=0.11, p=.74). Largest single gain +8.7%, not significant (chi2=1.94, p=.16, Llama 3-8B on CommonsenseQA). Recomputed from the original paper: average-of-all-stimuli relative gain 4.42% on BIG-Bench and 2.58% across all benchmarks, vs 115% for best stimulus. Sandbagging replication also failed (-1% for both user biographies). Re-Reading replicated only for Llama 3 models.
limits: Different models and tasks from the original (conceptual replication); omitted the 'Are you sure?' stimulus; chi-square tests on benchmark subsets; no math-only analysis.
agent_relevance: Closes GAP 4: EmotionPrompt does not survive on 2024 models, and the original headline is best-of-eleven. Downgrade claim K05 to contested.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Training-free early exit: at reasoning transitions the model is asked for a trial answer and exits if its confidence is high. This is a verification-style stop rule. It beat a token-budget prompt (TCC, with the budget set to DEER's own length), Dynasor-CoT, Chain-of-Draft and NoThinking on accuracy at similar or lower length.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B overall: vanilla 64.2 acc; TCC 67.1 at 83.0% length; Dynasor-CoT 68.2 at 83.7%; DEER 69.2 at 61.5%. AIME24 vanilla 41.7 (13,765 tokens), TCC 48.4 (10,603), DEER 49.2 (9,839). Qwen3-14B overall DEER 83.7 at 57.1% length vs vanilla 82.8. QwQ-32B DEER 84.0 at 80.9% vs vanilla 82.6; TCC 80.4 at 99.7% (model ignored the budget). Across models: accuracy +0.9 to +4.8, length -19.1% to -42.9%.
limits: Budget baseline is a prompt-level token limit, not true s1 Wait forcing; no matched-token sweep against a fixed cutoff; single runs on small sets like AIME24 (30 items); reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: Partly closes GAP 3: stop-on-confident-trial-answer beat prompt token budgets at lower length. This is not the same as budget forcing that extends thinking.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Efficiently scaling LLM reasoning with Certaindex (Dynasor)
finding: Intermediate answers of reasoning models stabilise before the end. Certaindex measures this stability and drives early exit and token allocation. Same accuracy with fewer tokens.
numbers: Token savings 11 to 29% at equal accuracy for CoT; for the top 10% of problems 34% on AIME and 53% on MATH500; top 1%: 53% and 81%. Up to 50% compute saving and 3.3x throughput in serving. DeepSeek-R1 observed using about 3x more tokens than needed.
limits: Stability is reported regardless of whether the answer is ultimately correct, so the stop rule can lock in a wrong answer; savings are against the same model's full run.
agent_relevance: Evidence for a stop rule based on answer stability, a cheap variant of verification. Reconciles overthinking with persistence if the rule stops only once the answer has stopped changing.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning models know when they're right: probing hidden states for self-verification
finding: A probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct, with calibrated scores. Using the probe as a verifier to exit early cut tokens at unchanged accuracy.
numbers: Threshold 0.85: accuracy 88.2% (same as no early exit), about 24% fewer tokens. Threshold 0.9 or higher: 88.6% accuracy (identical), 19% fewer tokens. R1-Distill-Llama-8B.
limits: Needs white-box hidden states and a trained probe; one model family in the early-exit test; not an API-only method.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that the model has an internal am-I-right signal it does not use; a verification-based stop is feasible. For a black-box agent the analogue is a separate verifier pass, not tested here.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does thinking more always help? Mirage of test-time scaling in reasoning models
finding: Pushing reasoning models to think longer (Wait style) first raises then lowers accuracy. They explain it as variance: extra thinking raises output entropy, which looks like gains and then hurts. Parallel thinking with majority vote at the same budget beats extended thinking.
numbers: One model on a GSM-style set: accuracy 82.2 to 87.3 as thinking grew, then fell from 87.3 to 70.3 when tokens went from 1100 to 15,980. MATH-500 example: 83.2 standard vs 78.3 with forced extension. At a 16K budget parallel thinking gave up to 22% higher accuracy than sequential (abstract says up to 20%).
limits: Mechanism is a probabilistic model; results vary by model and dataset; forced extension, not natural persistence.
agent_relevance: Partly closes GAP 3 against budget forcing: at equal tokens parallel samples plus a vote beat longer single chains. Persistence should be bounded and verified, not pure length.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses the model's own token confidence to drop low-quality reasoning traces during or after generation, a confidence-based stop for individual traces. Fewer tokens than full parallel voting, with equal or better accuracy.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B on AIME 2025: DeepConf@512 up to 99.9% vs 97.0% majority vote (cons@512) vs 91.8% pass@1; up to 84.7% fewer generated tokens than full parallel thinking.
limits: Open models only; compared with 512-trace voting, not with budget forcing or a fixed cutoff at equal tokens; AIME 2025 has 30 problems.
agent_relevance: Confidence-based trace termination is the strongest current evidence that stopping bad paths early beats running everything to length. Links to abandon rules and S6 stop rules.

source: Gema et al. (2025, TMLR) Inverse scaling in test-time compute
finding: Tasks where longer reasoning lowers accuracy. Five failure modes: Claude is increasingly distracted, o-series overfits to problem framing, spurious correlations, loss of focus on deduction, and amplified concerning behaviour.
numbers: Claude Opus 4 on counting with distractors: near 100% falling to about 85-90% as reasoning extends. DeepSeek R1 natural overthinking: 70% to 30% with five distractors. A trend counts only if change exceeds 2% with non-overlapping CIs.
limits: Synthetic tasks built to cause inverse scaling; many models flat or noisy.
agent_relevance: Persistence has a cost: longer thinking can raise distraction. Counter-evidence to a blanket keep-going rule; supports a verification-gated stop.

source: Laban et al. (2023/2024) Are you sure? Challenging LLMs leads to performance drops in the FlipFlop experiment
finding: Ten LLMs, seven classification tasks, five challenger phrases such as Are you sure?. Models flip often and lose accuracy. Fine-tuning on synthetic challenge data reduced but did not remove the drop.
numbers: Average flip rate 46%; average accuracy drop 17% (the FlipFlop effect); fine-tuned Mistral-7b deterioration reduced by about 60%. Models: GPT-4, Claude V2, Gemini-Pro, Mistral and others.
limits: Classification tasks not math proofs; 2023 models; a reflect-then-decide step was not tested as a mitigation, only fine-tuning.
agent_relevance: Partial on GAP 6: no study found that tests re-verify-before-changing. The tested mitigation is training, which a scaffold cannot do. A scaffold rule (require new evidence before a flip) remains untested.

source: Fanous et al. (2025) SycEval: evaluating LLM sycophancy
finding: ChatGPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-Pro on 500 AMPS math questions and MedQuad. Rebuttals made models change answers, sometimes to correct ones (progressive) and often to wrong ones (regressive).
numbers: Sycophancy in 58.19% of cases (Gemini 62.47%, Claude 57.44%, ChatGPT 56.71%). Progressive 43.52%, regressive 14.66%. Preemptive rebuttals 61.75% vs in-context 56.52% on AMPS (Z=5.87, p<0.001). Persistence of sycophantic behaviour 78.5% (CI 77.2 to 79.8). Rebuttal text written by Llama 3 8B.
limits: Mid-2024 models; LLM-as-judge with 20 human-checked AMPS labels; rebuttals are templated.
agent_relevance: Persistence under social pressure: a 14.7% regressive flip rate overall. Progressive flips show not all changes are bad, so the rule must be evidence-gated, not never-change.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Large language models can self-correct with key condition verification (ProCo)
finding: Verify-then-correct without external feedback: mask a key condition in the question, add the current answer, ask the model to recover the condition, and revise if it does not match. Beats plain self-correction.
numbers: With GPT-3.5-Turbo: NQ 40.3 CoT, 40.1 Self-Correct, 48.0 ProCo; AQuA 48.7 Self-Correct vs 65.2 ProCo (abstract says +16.5 over Self-Correct); CSQA +9.6; GSM8K table reads 78.6 CoT, 75.1 Self-Correct, 87.1 ProCo (column labels garbled in PDF text; treat as indicative).
limits: Needs a question with a maskable condition; text extraction did not resolve which model each GSM8K column is; authors' own results only. Huang et al. showed intrinsic self-correction fails, so this is a different, structured check.
agent_relevance: Candidate for GAP 6: a structured re-verification (substitute and check) rather than are-you-sure. Gains over unstructured self-correction suggest a flip should need a verification that can fail.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) ELEPHANT: measuring and understanding social sycophancy in LLMs
finding: Social sycophancy (preserving the user's face) in 11 models including GPT-5; still high. Not a math benchmark.
numbers: LLMs preserve user face on average 45 pp more than humans; validate users 72% vs 22%; affirm both sides of a moral conflict in 48% of cases. Existing mitigation limited; steering promising.
limits: Open-ended advice, not reasoning; no flip-under-challenge test on math.
agent_relevance: GAP 8 stays open for math persistence: newer models were measured on social sycophancy, not on flip rate or give-up on math. Do not read the 2023 flip numbers as current.

source: Hecht, Bryan & Yeager (2023) A values-aligned intervention fosters growth mindset-supportive teaching and reduces inequality in educational outcomes (PNAS)
finding: A 45-minute online teacher module aligned with teachers' own values changed teaching practice and raised achievement in socioeconomically disadvantaged classes. A candidate moderator for the Yeager vs Macnamara split: the effect depends on context and on whether the environment supports the mindset.
numbers: 155 teachers got the module, 164 control, about 11,500 students. Abstract-level only: substantially improved achievement in disadvantaged classes. Effect size not retrieved (full text blocked, HTTP 403).
limits: Read from an abstract summary only; effect sizes not seen; same research group as the Nature study.
agent_relevance: Part of GAP 9: moderators are environment support and baseline risk, not the message alone. Agent analogue: a prompt backed by concrete moves (checkpoints), not a pep-talk line.

source: Burnette et al. (2023) meta-analysis of growth mindset interventions: for whom, how, why; Tipton et al. (2023) on meta-analysis practice; Rege et al. (2021) mindset and challenge-seeking
finding: Bibliographic record only (Crossref). Burnette et al. is the main meta-analysis on moderators, Tipton et al. argues mindset meta-analyses should model heterogeneity, and Rege et al. studies challenge-seeking as a mechanism.
numbers: No numbers read. Burnette Psychological Bulletin 149(3-4):174-205; Tipton Psychological Bulletin 149(3-4):229-241; Rege American Psychologist 76(5):755-767.
limits: Abstracts not retrieved; cannot cite effect sizes. Kept as leads for a later pass.
agent_relevance: GAP 9 stays partly open: moderators named in the titles (for whom, challenge-seeking) are not verified. Do not mimic challenge-seeking framing until read.
